title: A Nice Little Routine
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane describes a new piece of his lesson-opening routine: after a short Do Now, he runs a flexible mini-whiteboard segment that serves rotating purposes depending on the day, reinforcing a commonly-missed Do Now question with targeted practice rather than a verbal reminder, reviewing prior content in small spaced chunks rather than saving review for the end of a unit, checking exit-ticket understanding again the next day to catch false positives from same-day recall, checking prerequisite knowledge before it's needed, previewing upcoming topics weeks in advance so they're not encountered cold, and reinforcing foundational facts like multiplication that are worth continual light practice. Kane is explicit that he doesn't run all of these in one lesson, the time and focus flex depending on what the rest of the lesson needs, and that the routine has changed how he thinks about lesson sequencing generally, moving away from seeing each lesson as a discrete unit and toward seeing lessons as blending into each other via constant spaced review and preview. He credits the routine's inspiration partly to ideas from Direct Instruction, adapted to his own context rather than implemented as DI prescribes it.
points: Kane's targeted-practice fix for missed Do Now questions replaces verbal re-explanation ('remember, multiplying by one half is the same as dividing by 2') with a few minutes of whiteboard practice, arguing practice sticks where reminders don't.

He distinguishes exit tickets from next-day recall checks, arguing exit tickets can give false positives because students can perform a skill minutes after seeing it without the knowledge actually sticking.

He previews upcoming content weeks ahead of the unit that needs it (e.g., inequality symbols two weeks before an inequalities unit), using small daily doses rather than a single dense pre-teach session.
His biggest conceptual shift is moving from seeing lessons as discrete chunks to seeing each lesson as blending into the one before and after via continuous, flexible spaced review.
quotes: I still start each class with a five-question Do Now. It’s fast, I aim for three minutes flat.

Before when a lot of students got a Do Now question wrong I did something that didn't work very well... Instead, I note the mistake and add a clarification and a few quick problems to our whiteboard work.
If lots of students struggle on an exit ticket, I know I need to reteach that. But exit tickets can also give false positives.
The spaced practice helps that knowledge stick way better than if I try to do it all the day of.
One way this has changed how I look at teaching is that I see lessons less as discrete chunks to teach and then move on. Each lesson blends into the lesson before and the lesson after.
I'm doing all the things I always mean to spend time on but never get to.
